name: Axillary sweat gland suction

card.summary: Surgical removal of underarm sweat glands through small incisions, with only small registered trials behind it in our sources.
card.note: Surgical procedure; outcome data in available sources are sparse.

quick.overview:
Axillary sweat gland suction is a minor surgery in which armpit sweat glands are removed or disrupted using suction or curettage. It is used for heavy underarm sweating and sometimes for underarm odor.

Only small registered trials appear in the available record, without published results.
quick.mechanism: Physically removing or destroying the glands means they can no longer produce sweat.
quick.risks: Surgical risks apply in general; specific complication data were not available in the reviewed sources.

lead: Axillary sweat gland suction, also called suction-curettage or liposuction-type removal, is a minor surgical approach to underarm sweating and underarm odour in which sweat glands in the armpit are physically removed or disrupted through small incisions.[1][4] People pursue it for drier underarms, less odour and fewer sweat marks on clothing, which affects how fresh and confident they look and feel in close contact and in light-coloured shirts.

Wikipedia's hyperhidrosis article lists axillary sweat gland removal or destruction by suction, curettage, liposuction-type removal or laser ablation among surgical options.[1] Related procedures are used for axillary osmidrosis, the medical term for pronounced underarm odour, where apocrine glands, which secrete compounds that skin bacteria turn into odorous substances, are the main target.[3][5]

A 2020 meta-analysis of 8 studies and 1,179 patients compared closed suction-curettage with open excision of the apocrine glands for osmidrosis. It reported high satisfaction after both approaches and a significantly lower risk of acute moderate-to-severe adverse events after the closed approach, while open excision had a lower recurrence or ineffectiveness rate overall.[4]

chain: Sweat glands removed or disrupted through small incisions
Drier underarms and fewer sweat marks
angle.text: The procedure removes or breaks up the glands that produce underarm sweat and odour, so the underarm area stays drier and smells less. It is done by a surgeon through small incisions.

infobox: Antiperspirants, botulinum toxin, open excision, laser[1][5]

paras: Surgical approaches remove or destroy the glands rather than blocking their nerve signal. Reference sources group suction, curettage and laser ablation together as axillary gland procedures.[1]

Underarm odour arises mainly from bacteria acting on secretions of the apocrine glands, and genetics such as the ABCC11 gene influence odour-producing secretions.[5] Non-surgical options include aluminium chloride antiperspirants, deodorants, antibacterial soaps and, for severe sweating, nerve-cutting surgery.[5]

In the 2020 Annals of Dermatology meta-analysis of osmidrosis surgery, pooled data showed open excision to be significantly more effective than closed suction-curettage overall (odds ratio 2.90 for ineffectiveness with closed surgery), but the difference was not significant when only studies with at least three months of follow-up were analysed. The authors suggested that efficacy should be judged at six months or later because recurrence was reported after that point.[4]
Reported satisfaction was roughly 88 to 98 percent for closed surgery and 78 to 98 percent for open surgery, a difference that was not significant.[4]

In the same meta-analysis, closed suction-curettage carried a significantly lower risk of acute moderate-to-severe adverse events than open surgery (odds ratio 0.15). Skin necrosis was more frequent with open surgery and wound dehiscence occurred only with open surgery, while haematoma rates did not differ significantly.[4] The authors summarised closed surgery as safer but less effective than open surgery, based on a small number of mostly non-randomised studies.[4]

A registered trial (NCT01274611, 20 participants, started 2010) studied botulinum toxin and suction-curettage for axillary hyperhidrosis.[2] Another registration (NCT01539460, 30 participants, started 2012, status unknown) examined combined liposuction with subcutaneous pruning for axillary osmidrosis.[3] Results of these registrations are not described in the available record.
Beyond these registrations, the 2020 meta-analysis pooled 8 mostly non-randomised comparisons of closed and open surgery for osmidrosis, as summarised above.[4]

timeline.event: Trial of botulinum toxin and suction-curettage for axillary hyperhidrosis begins (NCT01274611).[2]
Trial of liposuction with subcutaneous pruning for axillary osmidrosis begins (NCT01539460).[3]
Meta-analysis of open versus closed surgery for axillary osmidrosis published in Annals of Dermatology.[4]
